topSkills: Strategy • Product Management • Project Management • People Management
about:
At Citi, Kurt drives global product design excellence by optimizing processes that enhance efficiency, collaboration, and impact across Product, Technology, and Business teams. He develops and implements strategies that streamline workflows, accelerate project delivery, and uphold consistent design quality for a globally distributed team spanning India, Singapore, California, New York, Chile, Mexico, Toronto, and the UK.

Before Citi, Kurt was a Product Management Director at Prudential Financial, where he led the development and launch of award-winning products and websites for Workplace Solutions and Prudential Global Investment Management. His work prioritized accessibility, customer satisfaction, and data-driven decision-making to create seamless, scalable processes. Earlier in his career, Kurt built digital products as a technology, financial services, and sports product manager, working with firms like PriceWaterhouseCoopers and American Express. 

Outside his work life, Kurt has been the president of one of the world’s largest Toastmasters clubs and a certified Head Coach for the Special Olympics New York powerlifting team. An athlete himself, he’s competed in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, Olympic weightlifting, and natural bodybuilding. He was a nationally ranked powerlifter and two-time record holder.

He earned a BA from UCLA and an MBA from Baylor University—and continues learning every day.

I have 20+ years experience as a Solutions Architect and Dev Team Lead in Fortune 100 LOB App Dev, and helped craft solutions in diverse industries & sectors at JPMC, Microsoft, Pfizer, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, among others.

In my current role, I built, mentor, and manage the team that develops and maintains our entire software stack and serverless cloud infrastructure consisting of a 3NF & NoSQL backed API, SPA, various web clients, and federated API integrations with external partners, all of which were architected by me. I selected, designed and maintain the cloud infrastructure that is highly scalable and exceedingly cost efficient, and I established the CI/CD infrastructure for our agile process we follow as a dev team that values modern software engineering practices, security best practices and constant improvement and removal of technical debt to better achieve the company's strategic and tactical goals.

My work has taken me across industries including finance, beauty, and retail. I’ve designed and led leadership development strategies that create real change and earn the trust of senior leaders. What matters to me is making learning practical, measurable, and tied directly to what the business needs to achieve.

Today, I lead global instructional design at Citi, where my focus is on building programs that help people grow and drive stronger business performance.

My strengths include:

- Strategic learning design that drives results

publications.title: The Impact of Lecture Webcasts and Student Self-Regulated Learning on Academic Outcomes
publications.publishedAt: 9th Annual Blended Learning Conference and Workshop · Apr 23, 2012
publications.description: This presentation will explore the role of self-regulatory dimensions such as intrinsic learning orientation, self-efficacy, help-seeking, effort regulation, peer learning, task value, test anxiety and time and environment management, and how these dimensions are related to viewing time on online lecture webcasts, lecture attendance, and other course components. These patterns will then be related to academic outcomes (e.g., final grades). Additionally, this presentation will examine students' webcast viewing patterns and the extent to which the webcast viewings contributed to their overall grades in the course. Some questions include: what are the patterns of lecture webcast viewing across the semester? What are the correlations between academic outcome and webcast viewing for highly resourceful students and how does this differ for less resourceful students?

Seatrain Lines, Inc. was a major (NYSE-Listed) U.S. shipowner / operator active in the Americas and trans-Pacific trades. In the late 1960s Seatrain expanded into the North Atlantic trades, whereupon two new (chartered) high-speed gas turbine-powered German-built container ships were added to their fleet – “Seatrain Euroliner” and “Seatrain Eurofreight”. At this same point in time the company entered into the shipbuilding arena, as well. In the wake of the disastrous venture into shipbuilding, compounded by OPECs price increases during the mid-1970s (elevating the price of bunker), Seatrain was compelled to rapidly divest itself of chartered tonnage to cut it’s losses in the North Atlantic. Poor business decisions and an adverse geopolitical climate ultimately brought about a state of “Bankruptcy”.
Egon Cholakian was brought into the Seatrain demise as a Financial Overseer (Master) in furtherance of repatriating “Seatrain Euroliner” and “Seatrain Eurofreight” back to their owner(s) in the midst of a complex bankruptcy action.

During the early 1980s, Eurobridge Transport Limited, a non-vessel owning common carrier (NVOCC), was operating three non-conference German flagged vessels on the North Atlantic (at a time when North Atlantic trade was severely depressed), and two (limited) time-chartered vessels on the Pacific. In turn, Eurobridge was encountering difficulties meeting financial obligations with the Hamburg DE based shipowning consortium. As the German shipowners were not anxious to repatriate the vessels (realizing it would likely be difficult to reposition the ships with other potential charter parties in a depressed market), and; given that Eurobridge Transport Limited no longer possessed the credit-worthiness to secure replacement ships, it was necessary to bring in a Financial Overseer (Master) to navigate the awkward situation.

Egon Cholakian was brought into the Eurobridge Transport Limited disposition matter as an independent Financial Overseer, by mutual consent of all shipowning / operating parties – with full discretionary authority.

__________

During the early 1980s, Eurobridge Transport Limited, a non-vessel owning common carrier (NVOCC), was operating three non-conference German flagged vessels on the North Atlantic (at a time when North Atlantic trade was severely depressed), and two (limited) time-chartered vessels on the Pacific. In turn, Eurobridge was encountering difficulties meeting financial obligations with the Hamburg DE based shipowning consortium. As the German shipowners were not anxious to repatriate the vessels (realizing it would likely be difficult to reposition the ships with other potential charter parties in a depressed market), and; given that Eurobridge Transport Limited no longer possessed the credit-worthiness to secure replacement ships, it was necessary to bring in a Financial Overseer (Master) to navigate the awkward situation. Egon Cholakian was brought into the Eurobridge Transport Limited disposition matter as an independent Financial Overseer, by mutual consent of all shipowning / operating parties – with full discretionary authority. Egon CHOLAKIAN ultimately repatriated the vessels in behalf of the German shipowners.

about:
As a Senior Vice President at Citi with over three years of experience in the role, the focus has been on managing the cost of credit P&L for a $210 billion diversified portfolio. This involved delivering earnings narratives, benchmarking materials, and P&L projections to support high-level CFO/CEO decision-making, strategic planning, and new business development. Collaborating across teams, the efforts have consistently driven returns above the hurdle rate, supporting inorganic growth initiatives.  

Previous leadership roles at Citi included managing an $11 billion retail partner portfolio, refining credit strategies, and implementing machine learning models for precise target segmentation. These experiences underscore expertise in financial modeling, data-driven decision-making, and cross-functional collaboration to enhance profitability and mitigate risks. Passionate about leveraging finance and technology to deliver impactful outcomes.

Industry focus: Financial Services, Retail, E-commerce, Healthcare, Technology (Software and Semiconductor), Enterprise IT

Functional areas: Portfolio Management, Finance, Business Strategy, Data Science, Market Research, R&D, New technology and Product Commercialization, Credit and PE/VC market

Interests: Gen AI, Agentic AI, Blockchain, Ethereum, Crypto, web3.0, DeFi, and Fintech

publications.title: Don’t Hold Your Breath: A Protagonist’s Poetic Catharsis
publications.publishedAt: From The Heart Publishing · Aug 1, 2018
publications.description:
Each day we wake up and perform on the stage of our lives. In doing so, we develop the need to express the hidden thoughts conceived in our minds about our relationships; thoughts of longing for love, feelings of love, loss of love, and the liberty of loving ourselves. This book gives you the opportunity to express yourself! "Don't Hold Your Breath!" has its origin in the annual slumber party I used to give for my closest girlfriends when I lived in New York. We would eat the most fattening foods that we avoided all year long, share tiny morsels of gossip, and reveal the juiciest parts of our reality. It was our time to lay down our degrees, let down our defenses, and just be open and honest with each other about our lives. It was a time for defining our troubles, expressing our fears, soothing our wounds, and renewing our spirits. As young women, we were diverse in our backgrounds and careers, however we shared a common link. We held our breath in hopes of Mr. Right and the subsequent relationship that would ensue. Some of us were found by Mr. Right, and some of us found Mr. Right-Now, however we continued to hold onto the truth; “Boyfriends, lovers, and husbands come and go, but your girlfriends, they are forever!”

https://www.amazon.com/Dont-Hold-Your-Breath-Protagonists/dp/1983301671/ref=tmm_pap_swatch_0?_encoding=UTF8&qid=1610155541&sr=8-13

publications.title: The Sangrita Club - a novel
publications.publishedAt: 220 Communications · Jan 1, 2016
publications.description:
Four New York City female corporate executives: Vanessa, Anne, Monica, and Maria come from differing backgrounds, racially, culturally and socioeconomically, and struggle with varying issues of abandonment, lovelornness, sexual abuse, and addictions. At first glance, it appears as though they have nothing in common, however as members of The Sangrita Club, these women discover that they are all seeking the same thing, a way to escape.
The Sangrita Club is a story of how these women forge a bond in the face of adversities, which helps them find a way up, out, through, around, and over the stumbling blocks in their lives and transform them into stepping-stones.  By breaking through each other’s facades, they discover the illuminating value that lies within their sisterhood, which helps them heal from the symptoms of their past secrets.

https://www.amazon.com/Sangrita-Club-Amanda-Adams/dp/1684197791/ref=tmm_pap_swatch_0?_encoding=UTF8&qid=1610154861&sr=8-1

Career Highlights:
In my current role as Senior Vice President – Head of Enterprise Analytical Services Platforms Operations at Citi, I am responsible for implementing and operationalizing the global Big Data Hadoop ecosystem. My achievements include managing Citi's labor budget of $14MM/year and an indirect capital hardware/software budget of $200MM. I lead a direct team of 124 resources spread globally, overseeing everything from Cloudera CDH environment establishment to building strong support services for Big Data within Citi.

slides.title: A Fresh Perspective on Corporate Sustainability for the U.S.
slides.subtitle: Ainsley Cathcart, CAMS on LinkedIn
slides.description: Three weeks ago, I had an incredible opportunity to attend an exchange program at Copenhagen Business School taught by Dr. Robert Strand with other MBA students from the U.S. The program was titled “Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and Sustainability in Scandinavia.” While I am personally passionate about CSR and sustainability, the topic was relatively new to me from a business strategy perspective. While in Copenhagen, I learned a great deal about effective strategies that promote sustainability and profitability, and was able to experience firsthand the attributes of the Scandinavian culture which enable them to be global leaders in this area. It quickly became evident that there are key differences between the United States’ and Scandinavia’s approach to CSR and sustainability as reflected in their contrasting dominant business management strategies and cultural values. U.S. strategic management has traditionally focused on competition and achieving “competitive advantage.” This was widely popularized through Michael Porter’s “Five Forces” model, which is arguably the leading business strategy model taught at business schools across America (refer to Figure 1). As Robert Strand points out in his 2018 working paper, "Open Innovation in the Nordics: Realizing the Potential," the Five Forces model depicts a “hyper competitive view of the firm that includes terminology indicative of military and war traditions such as "rivalry amongst existing competitors," "threat of new entrants," and "bargaining power of suppliers" [italics added for emphasis].” This model encourages a hypercompetitive environment in which firms compete not only with other businesses, but also with their suppliers, customers, employees, and regulators. In addition, in the U.S., focus is largely placed on optimizing short-term financial performance, while the broader influences that govern a business’ longer-term success are ignored or rarely considered. As Porter and Kramer note in their article, "Creating Shared Value" (2011), how else could corporations overlook the welfare of their customers, the depletion of natural resources vital to their businesses, the sustainability of key suppliers, or the economic distress of communities in which they produce or sell? The production of food, for example, has several hidden costs that are regularly overlooked – costs to the environment, to the depletion of earth’s resources, and to public health and healthcare. Yet more often than not, these factors are not considered in corporations’ strategies (such as its sourcing practices, portion sizes, marketing practices). This short-term view and competitive nature of businesses has become deeply institutionalized in the U.S. business, political, and regulatory environment. Many would go so far as to argue that public companies that support a longer-term strategy are demonstrating irresponsible governance or even a breach of fiduciary duty, the assumption being that focusing on a short-term time horizon yields higher profits more quickly. Furthermore, incentives are created such that a short-term focus is rewarded. Whether a CEO sets a firm up for success 15, 30, 50 years in the future is rarely, if ever, considered when assessing the effectiveness or compensation of a CEO. In contrast, Scandinavian strategic management has long focused on effective cooperation and a heightened willingness and ability to cooperate with their stakeholders. Eric Rhenman’s depiction of a company in relation to its stakeholders is illustrated in his leading business strategy book, "Industrial Democracy and Industrial Management" (1968), through several overlapping ellipses that depict jointness of interests shared by the firm and its stakeholders (refer to Figure 2). This implies the interests of the firm are not in conflict or competition with its stakeholders, but that effective management depends upon the ability to cooperate across organizational boundaries. The emphasis is thus on collaboration and knowledge flows, which increase the likelihood of a firm’s success. This cooperation and collaboration ultimately enables greater innovation and the creation of shared value, which is needed to address society’s greatest sustainability challenges while simultaneously realizing business opportunities. An essential element of this alternative approach is the understanding that “shared value” is not about “sharing value” already created by firms. It is instead about expanding the total pool of economic and social value through collaboration and innovation. Interestingly enough, decades after publishing the Five Forces model, Porter acknowledged the need to shift attention away from competition between firms and their stakeholders towards cooperation. Porter now believes the concept of shared value has the power to unleash a next wave of economic growth, while resetting the boundaries of capitalism. The shift towards this mindset in the U.S. has begun. However, in order for it to be successful here there needs to be a better understanding and appreciation of the framework and values within which a cooperative environment can thrive. The Scandinavian context can serve as inspiration for this. I had the opportunity to visit four large corporations while in Copenhagen to learn first-hand how they incorporate CSR and sustainability into their businesses. What stood out was that each company has embedded CSR directly into their core strategy. It was not viewed as an afterthought or a cost, nor was its inclusion entirely altruistic. It was integrated in ways that produced both business and societal benefit. For example, Maersk, the largest shipping company in the world, has committed to halving food loss through investing in innovations in its transportation chain. This exemplifies the firm’s ability to leverage its core competencies to address a broader societal issue, while simultaneously creating shared value throughout the supply chain, and unlocking economic growth. Furthermore, certain cultural values and the level of engagement evident in Denmark enhance their ability to create shared value through a more cooperative mindset. Themes of trust, humility, and equality frequently came out during conversations and in business examples. These values support the development of partnerships with clients, vendors, and suppliers, and facilitate open and honest relationships with all stakeholders. This leads to tremendous opportunities for innovation and creation of shared value. The Scandinavian consensus-driven culture and ability to debate topics across all levels of an organization, coupled with their recognition that today’s societal issues are too great to be addressed by one person or company, also make it easier for issues like CSR to be discussed broadly, and for identified solutions or strategies to have buy-in from all stakeholders. Corporate structures, such as Danish Industrial Foundations and Cooperatives, further enable a firm to align its values and core strategy with a more long-term, sustainable view. These insights into Danish corporate culture took on a very personal tone for me on my last day. When my classmates and I learned that Malmo, Sweden was only an hour train ride from Copenhagen, naturally, we decided to venture into the new country for an evening to explore. We ended up at a trendy restaurant where a construction company was coincidentally throwing a work party. After a while, the well-dressed host of the event walked up to our table. He had just learned we were visiting from the U.S. to learn about CSR. “I’m counting on you,” he declared with equal parts sincerity and intensity, staring each of us in the eyes letting his gaze linger longer than usual to ensure his words sank in. “Really, I’m counting on you. We must reduce our carbon by 40% by the year 2030. There is no other option, it has to be done. And I can only do so much in my own country.” Even though he was throwing his company’s work party, that didn’t stop him from spending the next several minutes away from his colleagues to discuss sustainability and CSR with our table, eagerly answering our questions and providing insights into the Scandinavian business context. Although we were in a neighboring country, the insights he shared reiterated precisely what we had learned in the classroom and through our company site visits in Copenhagen, and further exemplified the passion for sustainability that permeates Scandinavia. This program has really opened my eyes to a how a corporation can embrace social responsibility and a sustainable approach, while simultaneously creating economic growth. This concept needs to be more widely understood as I strongly believe the future of our country and our world greatly depends upon it. We must engage as a movement, not just as an individual, not just as a company, and not even just as a nation. It up to each of us to initiate this movement in America. “ The greatest threat to our planet is the belief that someone else will save it” -Robert Swan Not sure where to start? Take a look at the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and determine towards which goal(s) your company can make an impact. SDGs act as common platform around which sustainability efforts can be targeted and formalized, providing a company with a common purpose. You can also check out this list of actions from the UN for things you can do in your everyday life. Every company has opportunities to create shared value, and their range and scope is far broader than has been realized so far. #StudentVoices #KelloggMBA #SustainableVikings #TheNordics #TracesOfNorth @robertgstrand @CBScph @NorthwesternUniversity-KelloggSchoolofManagement

about:
I have an extensive employment history, having worked in the banking industry for more than 17 years. 

I started my career as a Relationship Manager at The Bank of Mitsubishi Tokyo UFJ (formerly MUFG bank), where I worked for 5 years and was responsible for supporting mid-sized companies in Japan. 

Following this position, I moved to the Trade Finance team at UFJ Head Office in Tokyo, where I covered large-sized companies in the East and central areas of Japan for 2 years. 
After my tenure at Head office, I was assigned to work in New York in Trade Finance Sales.

Initially, I was engaged in building up the Global Trade Sales team, a new department for the bank, with locally-sourced team members. I was then placed in charge of all Japanese clients in North America, as the only Japanese national in the local team for almost 3 years. 

I had numerous responsibilities, including expanding the Trade and Finance business client base, as well as liaising with head office and the local team as a Japanese expat intermediary. 

I built strong relationships with my clients and closed significant deals, which later became a solid foundation for the team.

In 2018, I joined Citibank Tokyo in the Treasury and Trade solution sales department. 
I promoted Cash Management and Trade finance services for large-sized Japanese companies which are in the field of all C&H clients and TMT clients specifically. 

I spent two and a half years in Global Solution Sales in Japan, and provided a variety of diverse solutions that have enabled clients to streamline their internal work processes, making them more efficient. 

Since May 2021, I have been based in Singapore, and have undertaken a role at the Japan Desk/Treasury and Trade Solutions, covering all large sized Japanese companies in the APAC region.

Thanks to my extensive experience, I have confidence in trusting my performance in Relationship Manager and Transaction Banking Sales, and Cash and Trade roles globally.

In addition, I am actively working to expand my education, attending the Executive MBA program at The University of Chicago Booth School of Business since 2020. I am currently taking courses in Accounting, Corporate Finance, Private Equity Finance, Fin-tech and Corporate governance as well as General management at the University. 
I will graduate from Booth in 2022.

featured.title: The Fortress of Logic: The Vital Role of Defensive Programming
featured.subtitle: Marc Asher on LinkedIn

slides.title: The Fortress of Logic: The Vital Role of Defensive Programming
slides.subtitle: Marc Asher on LinkedIn
slides.description: In the modern digital landscape, software serves as the infrastructure for everything from global finance to medical equipment. As reliance on these systems grows, so does the cost of failure. While many developers are taught to write code that solves a specific problem—focusing on the "happy path" where inputs are correct and external systems function perfectly—reality rarely aligns with this ideal. This is where defensive programming becomes essential. Defensive programming is not merely a coding technique; it is a mindset that prioritizes stability, security, and maintainability by assuming that if something can go wrong, it eventually will. The primary argument for defensive programming is the assurance of system reliability. A non-defensive program is brittle; it operates under the assumption that users will always enter dates in the correct format, that network connections will never time out, and that files will always exist where they are expected. When these assumptions fail, the application crashes, leading to data loss and user frustration. Defensive programming mitigates this by validating all inputs and handling exceptions gracefully. By anticipating edge cases—such as a user entering text into a numeric field—a defensive programmer ensures the software provides a helpful error message rather than abruptly terminating. This robustness distinguishes professional-grade engineering from amateur scripting. Furthermore, defensive programming is inextricably linked to software security. Many of the most common vulnerabilities, such as SQL injection or buffer overflows, stem from a lack of defensive practices. When a developer implicitly trusts user input, they leave the door open for malicious actors to manipulate the system’s logic. Defensive programming operates on the principle of "never trust the user." By rigorously sanitizing inputs and enforcing strict boundary checks, developers can neutralize potential threats before they interact with sensitive core logic or databases. In this context, defensive coding is the first line of defense against cyber threats, protecting both the organization and its users’ privacy. To illustrate the practical difference, consider a critical operation: authenticating a user login. A naive implementation might construct a database query by simply gluing strings together, assuming the user will only enter valid text. This creates a massive security hole known as SQL Injection. In the naive example above, a malicious user can bypass authentication entirely by manipulating the input string to alter the database command. A defensive approach anticipates this malicious intent: Beyond immediate stability and security, defensive programming drastically reduces the long-term cost of software maintenance. In the software lifecycle, the majority of time and budget is spent not on initial creation, but on debugging and updating code. Non-defensive code often fails silently or generates obscure errors that can take days to trace. Conversely, defensive code is self-documenting regarding its constraints. Through the use of assertions and explicit error handling, the code reveals exactly where and why a state became invalid. This allows future developers—or the original author returning months later—to diagnose issues rapidly, saving countless hours of productivity. In conclusion, defensive programming is a critical discipline that elevates software development from a creative exercise to a reliable engineering practice. By anticipating failure, validating assumptions, and safeguarding against malicious intent, defensive programming ensures that applications remain robust in an unpredictable world. While it requires more effort and lines of code upfront, the return on investment is undeniable: software that is safer, more stable, and easier to maintain. In an era defined by digital dependency, defensive programming is not just a best practice; it is a professional necessity.

slides.title: Stop Asking 'Write X': Why AI Prompt Engineering is a critical skill for Career Resilience
slides.subtitle: Marc Asher on LinkedIn
slides.description: [Preface: I generated the following article in under 10 minutes using Gemini 2.5 Flash and only 4 refinements to my initial request. For those interested, message me and I will share the prompts I used to generate the article.] The Next Evolution of Programming: From Machine Code to Natural Language The history of computing is a relentless march toward greater abstraction, designed to make interaction with technology easier for human minds. Decades ago, programming required the precise, grueling syntax of machine code and assembly, demanding deep technical expertise and consuming massive amounts of time. The advent of high-level languages like C, Java, and Python provided the first major leap, allowing developers to write in human-readable logic. This was a massive productivity gain, but it still required mastering complex rules, compilers, and frameworks. Today, we stand at the precipice of the third, and arguably most democratizing, phase: Natural Language Programming. AI prompting bypasses technical syntax entirely, using the most universal human tool—language—to command highly sophisticated computing processes. Prompt engineering, therefore, is not merely a skill for AI models; it is the mastery of this new programming interface. The ability to precisely articulate intent in plain language is becoming the universal compiler for the modern knowledge worker. Following this evolution, Generative AI is establishing itself not merely as a technological trend, but as the new operating system for knowledge work. For every professional utilizing tools like Large Language Models (LLMs) or generative design platforms, the ability to create value is now intrinsically linked to one critical skill: AI prompt engineering. Defined as the deliberate practice of structuring inputs to elicit optimal, actionable output from an AI model, prompt engineering has transitioned from a technical niche to the essential interface between human strategy and machine power. Mastering this capability is rapidly becoming the single most important skill for driving productivity and ensuring career resilience in the modern economy. The Productivity Gap: Generic Input vs. Strategic Output At its core, prompt engineering is about converting vague human intent into precise, machine-executable instructions. The vast knowledge within an LLM is inert until activated by context, clarity, and constraint. As the IBM Institute for Business Value and other researchers confirm, the quality of the AI-generated content—whether it's code, market analysis, or a client pitch—is fundamentally determined by the quality of the prompt, a principle summarized simply as "good prompts equal good results" (IBM). The difference between a poorly structured query and a professionally engineered one defines the Productivity Gap. One approach wastes time and resources, while the other delivers immediate, high-leverage results. Poorly Crafted Prompt (Low ROI) "Write a report about renewable energy." (Vague task, no audience) Outcome: Generates a generic, 2,000-word academic overview requiring hours of editing to make it useful. Well-Crafted Prompt (High ROI) "Act as a sustainability consultant (Persona) and write a 500-word executive summary (Format/Constraint) for the CEO of a mid-sized utility company (Audience). The summary must analyze the financial viability of offshore wind power in the North Atlantic (Task), present three key findings in bullet points, and conclude with a specific, actionable next step (Structure)." Outcome: Produces a concise, targeted, professional document ready for immediate internal use, maximizing the model's efficiency and saving the user significant time. This comparison clearly shows that prompt engineering transforms the relationship from passively accepting a first draft to actively directing a professional deliverable. It moves the user from being a passive recipient of AI output to an active, strategic director of machine intelligence. This directional control is what generates genuine business value and competitive differentiation. The Mechanism of Mastery: Beyond Simple Keywords The techniques utilized by skilled prompt engineers go far beyond typing keywords. They employ structured methodologies to guide the AI’s thought process, ensuring complex tasks are handled reliably. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting: This involves instructing the model to "think step-by-step." For complex analytical tasks—such as auditing a contract or debugging a multi-layered software bug—CoT prompting forces the AI to reveal its reasoning before providing a final answer. This dramatically reduces 'hallucinations' and increases output reliability, transforming the AI into a verifiable collaborator rather than a black box. Few-Shot Learning: By providing 2-3 examples of a desired input/output pair (e.g., three examples of successful email subject lines and their corresponding email bodies), the prompt engineer can instantly fine-tune the model for style, tone, and specific formatting without expensive model retraining. This level of granular control is crucial for maintaining brand consistency in marketing and communications roles. Role Assignment and Context Priming: This involves assigning the AI a precise persona (e.g., "You are a senior mergers and acquisitions attorney") and providing specific background data (e.g., "The client’s goal is a 15% synergy reduction"). This deep context priming ensures the output is highly specialized, mitigating the risk of generic advice and making the AI's contribution immediately relevant to professional decision-making. The Universal Skillset: Roles Transformed by Prompt Fluency The benefits of prompt engineering are not confined to traditional tech roles; they are reshaping professional functions across the board. The ability to effectively direct generative AI is an accelerant for almost every knowledge worker, but its impact is most transformative in the following key job categories: 1. Creative and Content Professionals (Marketing Managers, Copywriters, Designers) For these roles, prompt engineering shifts the focus from tedious content creation to high-level strategy and refinement. A skilled marketing manager can use specific prompts to generate 50 targeted social media captions for five different platforms, adhering to a defined brand voice and campaign goal, in minutes. They move from drafting to editing, instantly scaling their creative output and allowing more time for audience analysis and strategic campaign oversight. The output here is not just fast; it is compliant and on-brand, thanks to precise linguistic constraints embedded in the prompt. 2. Technical and Engineering Professionals (Software Developers, Data Scientists, DevOps) In the technical domain, prompt engineering is becoming synonymous with efficient coding and system management. Software developers use it not just to generate boilerplate code, but to explain complex legacy systems, refactor old code into new paradigms, or quickly generate unit tests that cover edge cases. Data scientists use advanced prompting to create complex SQL queries, summarize research papers, or automate the initial stages of data cleaning and feature engineering, effectively elevating their role from manual laborer to high-level architect. The ability to articulate technical problems clearly is now directly proportional to coding speed. 3. Strategy and Management Consultants (Project Managers, Analysts, Executives) In high-pressure, decision-making environments, speed and synthesis are paramount. Consultants and strategists leverage prompt engineering to perform rapid market sizing, synthesize thousands of pages of quarterly reports into a concise executive brief, or conduct scenario planning based on complex variables. They prompt the AI to take multiple perspectives—for example, arguing for and against a merger from the vantage points of legal, financial, and regulatory risk. This dramatically accelerates the research and synthesis phase of projects, enabling quicker, more informed strategic decisions. 4. Operational and Support Roles (HR, Customer Service, Legal Support) Even operational roles are being redefined. HR professionals use engineered prompts to draft nuanced policy documents that comply with specific regional laws or to quickly summarize lengthy employee review cycles. In customer service, prompt engineering is used to build sophisticated internal knowledge-base chatbots that can handle highly specific and contextual queries, improving efficiency and first-call resolution rates. For legal support staff, the ability to prompt an AI to summarize case law and identify relevant precedents based on specific jurisdictional criteria is a game-changer for speed and accuracy. The Urgency of Career Resilience The urgency to master this skill is directly tied to job market dynamics. McKinsey estimates that generative AI has the potential to automate work activities that absorb up to 70% of employee time in knowledge-based roles (McKinsey). The individuals who will thrive in this environment are not those who resist the technology, but those who become its most fluent directors. Prompt engineers are the high-leverage collaborators. They serve as the quality control, the context-setters, and the strategic thinkers who ensure the AI’s output aligns perfectly with specific business objectives. In a future where everyone has access to the same powerful tools, the competitive advantage will go to the individual who can consistently extract better work, faster, using superior prompting techniques (Google Cloud). In conclusion, AI prompt engineering is not just another line item on a training budget—it is a foundational literacy that dictates your effectiveness, your output quality, and your future career trajectory. It represents the nexus of critical thinking, linguistic precision, and practical business strategy. As AI continues its rapid evolution, the core rule remains: the quality of your communication determines the quality of your career. Investing in prompt fluency today is the highest-leverage move a professional can make to secure a competitive edge tomorrow. References Google Cloud. Prompt Engineering for AI Guide. Accessed November 2025. IBM. What Is Prompt Engineering?. Accessed November 2025. McKinsey. What is prompt engineering?. Accessed November 2025.

slides.title: Musings on Motivation: Part 1
slides.subtitle: Marc Asher on LinkedIn
slides.description: For those who were not aware, I have had more free time the past several months due to corporate cutbacks driven by challenges in our industry, not the least of which was the Covid impact. While I miss the great teams I have had the opportunity to work with, I am also grateful for the chance to both learn and grow in other areas as well as share my insights with a larger audience as I grow my network. One topic that has been top of mind for me is motivation. As a leader, the question often comes up of how to motivate an employee to become more productive. Early in my career I was exposed to a simple concept that took me time to understand and internalize - you cannot create motivation in other people. Some people may hear this and immediately refute it by saying things like “If I offer my team a bonus to finish early, they will be more motivated”, or “If I threaten to fire someone for underperforming, that will motivate them to work harder”. The reality is that people come to you with their motivations already in place. For one person, their motivation may be financial security. For another, it may be a schedule that allows them more time with their family. I have had some team members who are driven by the challenge of solving difficult problems. Ultimately, to make each individual more productive and happier with their job, we need to understand both what motivation they come to us with and what we can do to align their work to their motivation. It is said that great leaders are also great listeners. If we understand that we cannot create motivation, and that each person may have a unique thing that motivates them, one of the key roles of a good leader is to learn what that motivates each person reporting to them. This is one of the areas where being a great listener is critical. While this is true in the work environment, it is something that is true in our personal lives as well (though as my wife will attest, a skill that I have not yet mastered). Once we understand each person’s motivation, our next challenge is how to meet them where they are and create an environment that appeals to their motivation. However, just the simple of act of letting them know that they are heard is a starting point to building a better relationship and more productive environment. Coming up: In my next installment, we will look at specific approaches that can be taken to learn and understand people’s motivations as well as some common motivators. Stay tuned!

slides.title: Musings on Motivation: Part 2
slides.subtitle: Marc Asher on LinkedIn
slides.description: In the first part of this series (https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/musings-motivation-part-1-marc-asher/), I talked about the fact that we cannot create motivation in others. As adults we come into any new environment or interaction, be it work or personal, with our own motivations in place. When it specifically comes to work, those motivations can range anywhere from seeking more compensation, personal recognition, intellectual challenge, available free time, or even doing a job that aligns with moral or ethical beliefs. The challenge I have personally faced as a leader is how to find out each individual’s motivation (or set of motivations). Unfortunately, we don’t all have neon signs on our foreheads that say “More money!” or “Career growth!”. Even if we did, the message that is shown may not be the whole story. For example, while an employee may ask for more money, it is possible their true motivation is personal recognition. They may see additional compensation as a way of having their work recognized, but if a raise is not accompanied by meaningful recognition of their work (such as letting the employee know specific contributions you have seen them provide), it will have limited positive impact on that employee. For those who have read Brené Brown (and if you haven't, I highly recommend you do so), there is a central theme that a) we are hard-wired for connection to others, and b) we build connection through vulnerability. While this does not mean I have to share my deepest darkest secrets with someone before they will be willing to let me in a little to see what motivates them, it does mean I have to be genuine. More so, if someone is going to take the effort and risk (and let's not kid ourselves, sharing something that we want to someone else always feels like a risk) to let you know what motivates them, as leaders we need to listen, learn, and not abuse their trust. As I stated in part 1, great leaders are great listeners. However, once we are done listening we then need to process what we have heard or observed. Listening is not just sitting and waiting for the other person to speak. It involves several techniques to elicit a conversation. While people may want to share information, nobody wants to talk to someone they feel is not paying attention or uninterested in what they have to say. There are lots of great books and website about how to engage in active listening, but it can mostly be distilled into a few simple points. No assumptions - do not go into a conversation with an assumption of what the other person is going to say or where the conversation will lead. Assumptions means you have already had the conversation in your mind without allowing the other person to participate. No distractions - if you want to connect with someone, they must know they are the most important thing while you are talking with them. While multitasking sounds great, it is one of the fastest ways to destroy connection. Repeat and confirm - when someone shares something of importance to them, make sure you understand it by repeating what you heard back to them. Simple phrases like "So if I understand what you are saying..." or "I can see how 'x' situation is making you feel 'y'." Obviously there is much more to being a good listener, but even running through a mental checklist of some of the basic points above before having a conversation can lead to a much more productive talk as well as help build better connections. For example, if I sit down with someone to discuss their career and the first thing they talk about is the activities they did with their family on the weekend, they are letting me know that quality family time is important to them. If I had already decided they wanted to talk about a new job role, I may completely miss that they are telling me what motivates them. Furthermore, if I am distracted and checking emails while that person is talking to me, without a word I have let them know I don't value them as a person or an employee. I can expect that regardless of whatever new job role or raise I might offer this employee, they will be looking to work somewhere else very soon. I recall a specific incident many years ago when an employee who was well compensated and doing excellent work was asked in passing by someone in a leadership position above him "Are you having fun?" It seemed like an innocuous question and the person asking it had already presumed the answer would be "Yes, of course!". However, our company (myself included) had not taken enough time to actually talk with this employee and understand what motivated them. In fact, they did want to have fun with what they were working on but they were not put in a position to work on projects that held their interest. When the question was asked but not in a way to engage real discussion, all it did was bring to focus for that employee that they were not doing what they wanted to do. That employee left the company shortly after and it was a learning experience for me that if we say we value our employees, we must understand what is important to them by actually making a connection with them. As a side note, one big challenge I have seen is when an organization states that it values it employees but then creates an unspoken rule that working excessive hours and putting work ahead of family and personal time is a badge of honor. Inconsistent messaging is yet another clear way to destroy connections. On the job site indeed.com, they have listed a concise summary of common motivations (https://www.indeed.com/career-advice/career-development/types-of-motivation). The article is targeted at job seekers to help them identify their own motivations and use them to further their career. However, it also provides a good set of examples for leaders to use to help understand and identify some common motivations. While I recommend looking at this list as a starting point, remember that people do not always neatly fall into one category or another. If there were a "one size fits all" solution, this would be simple. That said, the starting point is fairly simple, but is also often difficult. It starts with making connections. Coming up: In my next installment, we will look at different ways we can try to align work and the work environment to different motivating factors. Stay tuned!

projects.title: Michelin’s Manufacturing and Distribution Network
projects.associatedWith: Associated with Georgia Institute of Technology
projects.description: One of the requirements for the Master of Science in Analytics Degree is to complete a practicum project for a company. Our practicum project for Michelin involved using network optimization modeling to automate Michelin’s inventory management and shipping process of tires, while minimizing transportation costs and meeting customer demand. We started off by cleaning the data and performing exploratory data analysis on Michelin’s supply chain trends. We then developed a mixed-integer programming model in Python and performed analysis on the model output using visualizations. We finally presented our model, results, and recommendations to Michelin.

projects.title: Classifying Insects using Habitus Images
projects.associatedWith: Associated with Georgia Institute of Technology
projects.description: Created multiple machine learning models using both unsupervised and supervised learning methods to classify images of insects. The unsupervised methods included principal component analysis and k-means clustering. The supervised methods included a convolutional neural network and a decision tree. After preprocessing the data and building the models, we compared the different methods using a variety of machine learning metrics and found the convolutional neural network to perform the best.

projects.title: The All-In-One College Search Tool
projects.associatedWith: Associated with Georgia Institute of Technology
projects.description: Created a college recommendation tool that allows prospective students to find colleges that offer their major of interest. This tool was created using the US Department of Education College Scorecard dataset merged with the Equity in Athletics Dataset. Our tool allowed users to select a major, gave users the option to consider similar majors resulting from the k-means clustering algorithm performed in Python, and see the colleges that offer the major of interest on a Tableau visualization. The user can then filter the colleges by a variety of factors, such as test scores, athletics divisions, and location.

projects.title: Forecasting Slow-Moving SKUs - Best Buy
projects.associatedWith: Associated with Georgia Institute of Technology
projects.description: The Master of Science in Analytics program has a 2 week Data Science Project Competition sponsored by a company following the winter break. The problem Best Buy asked us to work on was to forecast units sold for 575 Best Buy products sold in small quantities, using a model with high accuracy and low runtime. After exploring and processing the data in Python, we implemented a gradient boosting model with runtime of ~9.3 seconds, r-squared of ~94.1%, and root mean squared error of ~4.5. At the end of the 2-week period, we presented our solution to Best Buy stakeholders using data storytelling techniques and won 4th place out of 21 Georgia Tech Master of Science in Analytics teams.

projects.title: Bike Demand Regression Analysis
projects.associatedWith: Associated with Georgia Institute of Technology
projects.description: Performed regression analysis in R that predicted demand of bikes using a Washington DC Capital Bike Sharing dataset. The analysis consisted of doing initial exploratory data analysis, checking for outliers and multicollinearity, performing variable selection, creating multiple types of models using training data, testing the models against a test dataset, checking model assumptions, and drawing conclusions.

projects.title: Forecast use of a city bikeshare system
projects.description: Our group analyzed the bike sharing system in Washington, DC. Core to this analysis, we predicted the total number of bike rentals by hour, throughout the day based on other variables. In our total data set there are a total of 17,379 rows (initially divided into 10,886 rows of training data and 6,493 rows of testing data) of hourly rental data spanning two years pulled from Kaggle. For my own part, I used the result of Principal Component Analysis as input and then Multivariate Regression to predict the count number.

projects.title: Florida Road Construction Bidding Collusion Inspection Regression Analysis
projects.description:
The data set contains information about 279 road construction contracts. It involves 3 qualitative variables and 11 quantitative variables.
The objective of this project is to help Florida Attorney General (FLAG) to inspect the suspicious bid collusion in the road construction bidding competition. By comparing the bid prices along with other significant bid variables, FLAG is able to establish invaluable benchmarks for detecting future bid-rigging. The contractor who submits the lowest bid price will win the contract of road construction. 
During the project, we tried to fit an appropriate regression model for predicting low-bid price. Our idea was to eliminate the irrelevant factors and build a regression model with the most significant variables. The model should be able to provide FLAG with useful information on the range of bidding prices. Therefore, our modeling process had three main steps: initial exploration of the data, regression model selection, model analysis and testing. The final model measures the change in price for every one-unit increase in each variable when the other independent variables in the model are held fixed. The predication and estimation values of the final model are also very close to real value for each trial. So FLAG will be able to use this model to get a range of estimation and prediction of bidding prices. The fair or competitive price of a contract should be in the range. If a bidder offers a price higher than the range, there may be a possibility of bid collusion.

projects.title: Wheat Kernels Data Mining
projects.description:
The examined data set comprises kernels belonging to three different varieties of wheat: Kama, Rosa and Canadian. It has total of 210 records with no missing value, randomly selected and evenly distributed into three varieties. For each of these records, we measure area, perimeter, compactness, length of kernel, width of kernel, asymmetry coefficient, and length of the groove. At the end of each record, we set 1, 2, or 3 as class label, indicating the variety that kernel belongs to. 
During the project, I used two clustering techniques to analyze and discover the pattern from the data set. The first approach of clustering is a partitioning tech called k-means clustering. The second approach is a hierarchical tech called hierarchical clustering. By comparison, I chose k-means algorithm as our best clustering method for this problem. It had a higher accuracy on prediction and clearly separated the clusters from each other.

projects.title: Video Rental Store Application
projects.description:
In this project, I built a PL/SQL-based application to insert and update records in a video rental store database and generate some reports. Functions of the application include:
• Add a new customer to the table.
• Update an existing customer’s expiration date.
• Search a video and display the information of the video’s copies. In addition, the due dates are also displayed for unreturned copies. The damaged copies are excluded in output.
• Record a new rental. When the video is successfully checked out, insert a new record into the table and update the corresponding record. A customer whose expiration date is less than the current date is not able to make a rental. 
• Change the rental status for returned copy. When the copy is successfully checked in, update both the rental table and the copy table. Otherwise, the action is denied.
• Retrieve all the copies that a customer hasn't returned. The output includes the customer's ID, name, expiration date, first checkout date, last checkout date, the number of unreturned copies, title, copy, format, rental date, and due date of the rentals.

Although our group was only there for one week, he quickly figured out people's skill sets (both tangible and intangible) and used each of us to the best of our abilities. We had a few group members with construction skills who he used like junior project managers, giving them greater freedom and responsibility on particular projects and conferring with them about different issues; others with limited skills but the confidence to complete a project when given enough guidance who he paired up with the junior project managers; and still another who didn't trust her own abilities who he used very effectively as an invaluable go-fer and comedic relief for other workers. 

I believe the best of Ricky's skills showed during a particular incident when our group members had a major disagreement. There was a scary moment when one of our members lost his head and that episode brought a major divide and uncomfortable feeling within the group. Ricky (younger than everyone in our group and young enough to be the son or grandson of most) calmed everyone down and brought the group back together when we were in danger of fracturing apart. I was humbled to see his composure in this situation and his ability to handle the many different personalities of a group of people whom he had only recently met.

If you are looking for a very poised, skilled, and caring project manager, I could not recommend anyone more highly than Ricky.

projects.title: "Forecasting Crime Rate using a Hybrid ARIMA and Neural Network Models: The Case of Normal, Illinois"​ | Tableau | R |
projects.description: This  paper  examines  the  effectiveness  of  a  hybrid  methodology  that  combines  both  time-series (TBATS) and Artificial neural networks (ANNs) models to predict crime rate in Normal, Illinois. The multi seasonal time-series model has been one of the most extensively used linear models in time  series  forecasting. Though,  the  time-series  model  is  not  certain to  capture  the  nonlinear patterns in the data, an artificial neural networks (ANNs) model is effectively used to capture the nonlinear patterns. Therefore, this study uses a hybrid approach that utilizes the unique strength of  both  the time-series  and  the  ANNs  models  to  forecast daily  crime  between  2010  -2014. The results  for  crime  data  indicate  that  by  using  the  combination  of  two  different  models  (hybrid model),  one  can   effectively   improve  the   forecasting  accuracy   and  achieve   better  results compared to the time-series and neural network models.

projects.title: “Predicting Insurance Claim Severity” | Machine Learning & Data Mining Methods | R |
projects.description: The purpose of this study was to conduct a statistical analysis to identify the best model which can predict the car insurance claim severity. The focus of this study was to examine each variable used in the model, and evaluate its impact on the loss claims. This was motivated based on the methods insurance companies use to determine the probability of claim severity. The study uses data from a competition on Kaggle website. Regression techniques, namely, OLS, best subset selection methods, shrinkage methods, dimension reduction methods, decision tree method, random forest method and boosting techniques (GBM) were used to predict the loss claim severity. The performance of each model was assessed using mean square error (MSE) and R-square. The results indicate that the random forest method was the best model to forecast claim severity.

projects.title: "Designing Paper Airplane"​ | Experimental Design Methods | Minitab | R |
projects.description: The paper investigates the performance of 32 airplane designs to determine which types Uncle Leo should recommend to his  nephew Fergus. For the purpose of the research we conducted an empirical study that analyzes the performance of each airplane design based on the distance and air time. The experiment not only  examines all categories, but also specifically compares each  design’s performance with the others’ 128 paper airplanes of 32 designs are thrown and measured including throwers’ height, hand use, distance, and air time. We provide the definitions of the best, better, and most enjoyable as the foundation of our research and analysis which helps us to answer  the research questions. The findings suggest that Basic Dart, Hunting Flight, and Heavy  Nosed  planes are the best performer in individual category. Overall, medium design is the best while Heavy-Nosed is the best design among all designs.

projects.title: “Investment and Portfolio Management: Trading Project” |  Stock Trak Virtual Trading Platforms  |
“Valuation Project and Company Analysis" ​ |  United Continental Holdings Inc. (UAL)  |  Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)  |  Excel  |
projects.description: In  view  of  our  analysis  of  the  United  Airlines (UAL),  it  is  recommended  that  the  shares  of  United Continental  Holdings  Inc.  should  be  bought or held.  This  recommendation  is  based  on  the  factors such  as  company  valuation,  financial  analysis  of  comparable firms,  and  sensitivity  analysis. Using capital asset pricing model (CAPM), the  value of the  firm  stock  is  equal to $639.34, which  is  significantly  more than the  current  trading  value  of  $54.80  per  share  (June  26,  2015).  In  addition,  the  estimates  using EV/EBITDA and P/E ratio analysis also indicate that the shares are underestimated. Overall, the findings for United Continental Holding imply that the company’s stock is undervalued; bearing that UAL  has  an  exceedingly  volatile growth pattern which  signifies  it as a  high risk company. As a result, we expect that investment in this company  is a  profitable opportunity provided that the investors are willing to take higher risk.

projects.title: "Illicit Drug Use and Labor Force Participation"​ |  Logistic Regression Model  |  STATA  |  SAS  |
projects.description: In this paper, I examined the question about how 2008 recession affected the relationship between illicit drug use and labor force participation. The data used to analyze the relationship between illicit drug use and labor force participation is obtained from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLS) – 1997. I have used the logistic regression model to examine the effects of recession on the relationship. I found no evidence in support related to the impact of 2008 recession on the relationship between marijuana and labor market status. However, I found convincing evidence to indicate that the hard drug use like cocaine is associated with high risk of unemployment. The treatment effect estimation results also indicate significant adverse effect of cocaine use on the individual employment status. However, given the results, I believe that policy decision should be mainly concerned with the implications of drug use regardless of the classification of different drugs and its impacts on labor market status.

projects.title: "The Effects of Fiscal Policy in Pakistan: VAR/VECM models"  |  Time Series Analysis  |  EViews  |
projects.description: This paper studies the effect of fiscal policy on GDP, net taxes, inflation rate (measured in GDP deflator), and  interest  rate  in  Pakistan  using  a  vector  autoregressive  model. As  the  fiscal variables indicate co-integration (long-term    relationship), therefore, the final model specification of VAR  is  estimated  as  error  correction  model  (VECM). The  data  of annual observations for fiscal variables of  Pakistan is used for the period of 1971-2013.Fiscal  policy shocks  are  identified as the structural residuals  related  to  unexpected  government  expenditure and  tax  revenues. Impulse  responses  are  then  used  to  simulate  the  dynamic  response  of  key macroeconomic variables to the shocks. The analysis shows a positive response of GDP to both expenditure  and  tax  shocks. However,  GDP  and  government  expenditure  reacts  negatively to inflation rate and interest rate. Altogether most of the variation in the variables is explained by the shocks in their own past history.

honorsAndAwards.title: Second Prize Winner for 2015/2016 Statistical Project Competition  |  Research topic: “Capital Mobility in Germany” | Time Series Analysis | R | EViews |
honorsAndAwards.issuedBy: Department of Mathematics, Illinois State University  -  URL:  http://math.illinoisstate.edu/actuary/casestudieslibrary.shtml
honorsAndAwards.description: This study evaluates the relationship between investment and savings in Germany over the period of 1971 to 2014. Using advance time-series estimation methods the findings reveal that the saving-retention coefficient is low, contradictory to the finding of Feldstein and Horioka (1980). Thus, result indicate high degree of capital mobility in Germany. The results for the sensitivity of investment to different forms of saving ratios suggest that the government savings is mostly invested domestically. While, private savings is inclined to be invested abroad. Furthermore, the effect of Maastricht treaty in 1992 indicate that the integration of European Union has increased dispersion between savings and investment ratios, and has negatively affected domestic investment. The overall results suggest that Germany can implement policies that emphasis on increasing investment through domestic savings by enhancing opportunities for private savers in the country.

I didn’t plan to become a risk manager. Growing up in Toronto, ‘risk manager’ wasn’t even a job I knew existed. But I liked the business section of the newspaper alright and I liked putting order to things. I liked knowing that things were fixed. That they were safe.

Fast forward a whole lot of years and here I am in the midst of enterprise risk management for a large Wall Street bank. With over 20 years of experience in the industry, I've honed my skills through more than one crisis. As an executive, I’m known as a bit of a change agent that can develop strategic target states and mobilize the firm for execution. People drive outcomes, so I spend the time to cultivate stakeholder relationships and build diverse, high-performing teams.  And good ideas need a podium, so I’ve gotten good at explaining risk issues to audiences that range from students all the way to the Board. 

I’m currently leading strategy and messaging for Citi's Enterprise Risk Management function and its risk and controls transformation, having joined the firm in 2007 (fortuitous timing for a risk manager!). Prior to Citi, I worked on the buy side in various and sundry roles, picking up degrees and certifications along the way. If you’re interested in collaborating on work that moves the profession forward and helps keep the financial system safe as houses, give a shout!

headline: Product Designer | UX Lead | B2B SaaS & Enterprise UX | HCI (IIT-B) | Design Strategy & Accessibility Advocate | Mentor | 18 yrs in Fortune 500 & Scalable Platforms
about:
Viraj Avachat is a Product Designer and Experience Design Leader with 17 years of experience crafting scalable, intuitive, and accessible digital products.

He brings deep expertise in end-to-end product design, from early user research and problem framing to prototyping, usability testing, and driving iterative improvements post-launch. Having led design initiatives across complex B2B domains such as Healthcare, Finance, Insurance, and Enterprise Tools, Viraj thrives in cross-functional teams where design, product, and engineering come together to solve real user problems.

In recent roles, he has led multi-disciplinary design teams, mentored junior designers, and owned the design of key product features from concept to launch. He has worked closely with product managers and engineers in Agile environments to drive feature adoption, usability improvements, and iterative refinements based on user research, feedback loops, and business metrics.

He holds a Master’s in Design (M.Des) with a specialization in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and a CEP certification from IIT Bombay, equipping him with a strong foundation in research-led design, cognitive psychology, and user-centered innovation.

He’s passionate about accessibility and has hands-on experience implementing AA/AAA WCAG compliance.

He is comfortable working in Agile product teams and experienced with design systems, complex information architecture, and user workflows, particularly in the B2B SaaS space.

Specialties: Product Design, UX Strategy, Design Leadership, Accessibility (WCAG), Enterprise UX, SaaS UX

experience.position: Author of Productive Accidents — a playbook for personal & professional adventure
experience.description:
Productive Accidents is my second self-published piece of work, but my first attempt at self-distribution. The book shows how a framework for curiosity and creativity can also be a recipe for innovation and adventure. There are ten actionable insights backed by examples that can be applied by individuals, families, or companies. The more you experiment with these ideas, the more you realise that serendipity can be a predictable and repeatable experience.

At a deeper level, Productive Accidents provides a way to maintain a growth mindset, build an authentic network, and contribute across a wide range of interests and causes. At the extreme it also provides a way to beat a midlife crisis, survive a tragedy, and live a playful and generous life. It might even be a remedy for regret.

receivedRecommendations.description: Peter has infectious energy and an ability to see potential in new ideas and new ways of thinking before most people do. Peter was a founding board member of Resolve and has done so much to promote its mission, vision and values and get its brand name out there. receivedRecommendations.givenByHeadline: The playbook is broken. I write about what comes next for leaders navigating complexity and collapse.
receivedRecommendations.givenAt: September 29, 2017, Dr. Richard worked with Peter B. but they were at different companies
receivedRecommendations.description:
Peter lives and breathes collaboration to a level I've rarely encountered elsewhere. He excels at putting open-minded people together and seeing what productive accidents extend from their interactions. 

The curation of productive accidents perhaps best describes what he does. Creativity and innovation rely on boundary spanning exercises - when people with diverse mind-and-skill sets come together to collaborate on creative and novel thoughts, ideas and practices. You can never predict what such people will produce in this domain crossing exercise. You just trust the process and wait for the magic to happen.. what they produce will be exciting, fresh and worthwhile. 

That's what Peter does. He identifies people who can make a difference and places them together with other people who can make a difference and sees what emerges from the other end. The results can be and are often outstanding. New cross-industry partnerships, academic-industry collaborations, novel artistic endeavours, meaningful social enterprises, and new ideas and practices that can generate energy and engagement in all those that encounter them.

The world needs to treasure people like Peter if it wants to take innovation and collaboration seriously. I would recommend him wholeheartedly for any position that involves running innovative and creative processes. You would rarely come across somebody better fit for such a role.

about:
There has been a consistent thread through each one of my roles at Citi: helping clients achieve a superior experience by connecting treasury innovation with their strategic objectives. From starting as an Associate in the post-MBA program, to managing global accounts as VP, to leading Treasury Solution Sales Officers as a Director, and now as Client Executive Team Lead, I’ve grown alongside clients across industries while staying true to what matters most - trust, collaboration, and meaningful results.

Today, I lead a team of six Client Executives (also known as Client Success Managers/CSMs), dedicated to safeguarding revenues, deepening relationships, and ensuring our clients maximize Citi’s full suite of treasury and trade solutions. I bring together my background in sales leadership, governance, and client advocacy with my passion for people development and team success.

Outside of work, I find inspiration in art, theater, and New York City’s creative energy. Whether exploring galleries, supporting queer artists, or catching the latest Broadway or Brooklyn production, I believe creativity fuels leadership. That balance between professional rigor and personal passion helps me bring fresh perspective, adaptability, and heart into my work for my team & clients.

I guide my team in leveraging Citi’s Treasury and Trade Solutions that includes Liquidity Management, Payments & Receivables, and Digital Channels & Data - to deliver high-impact, client-centered outcomes.
Key responsibilities include:

* Leading and developing a team of six CEs/CSMs to serve as trusted advisors across the Digital, Tech, Comms & Industrials sectors

projects.title: Magnetic Waves
projects.description: Magnetic fields are well known to be vitally important on the earth and in the whole universe. The Earth’s magnetic field protects our planet from the charged particles streaming out from the Sun in the form of the solar wind. Magnetic fields in outer space play a significant role in star formation. Magnetic fields are also extensively used in industry to control the motion of liquid metals. The study of the dynamics of magnetic fields in electrically conducting fluids, such as in plasmas, liquid metals, and saltwater, is called magneto-hydrodynamics, or MHD for short. In this project, we will investigate a few mathematical MHD models and perform simulations to visualize different types of magnetic waves. The models involved are 1-dimensional or 2-dimensional.

publications.title: 1D Model for the 3D Magnetohydrodynamics
publications.publishedAt: Springer · Jul 27, 2023
publications.description: We proposed a one-dimensional (1D) model for the three-dimensional (3D) incompressible ideal magnetohydrodynamics under Professor Mimi Dai's leadership. For this 1D model, local well-posedness is established, and a regularity criterion of the Beale–Kato–Majda type is obtained. Without the stretching effect, the model with only transport effect is shown to have global in time strong solution. Some numerical simulations suggest that solutions of the model with certain smooth periodic initial data are not likely to develop singularities in finite time, while solutions starting from other initial data have the tendency to form singularities.

headline: Banking & Wealth Management | Technology and Product Leadership | Digital Transformation | API Platforms and Ecosystems | Partnerships
about:
Well-rounded technology & product focused executive with 20+ years of experience in building, scaling & monetizing global digital platforms and product offerings in banking and telecom. Possess deep engineering expertise combined with product management, business strategy, P&L management skills to create value for customers, clients and the enterprise. 

Currently, I head up BBVA’s award winning Banking-as-a-Service platform pioneering open banking and embedded finance through strategic partnerships. Open Platform is run as an independent SaaS business and as the GM, I am responsible for all aspects of the platform business ranging from BD, product, engineering, client operations and risk & control functions. I guided Open Platform through market launch in 2018, subsequently scaling operations and exceeding revenues and KPI targets in 2019 and 2020.

Previously, I have held leadership positions at BBVA, Barclays, AT&T, Verizon in various engineering and product roles driving digital transformation agendas, new product launches and creating operational efficiencies. Every role has entailed building high performing global teams with a strong bias for execution and collaboration. 

Fortunate to have a global perspective and respect for cultures having lived/worked/visited US, Europe, Mexico, Latam and Asia.

Lifelong learner with a keen interest in industry, technology and innovation trends. I have an MBA (Chicago Booth) and MS (Baruch CUNY) and BTech (IIT Delhi) in engineering.

Direct responsibility for over 200 globally distributed program managers, project managers, release train engineers, L1,L2 and L3 support resources and scrum masters

Leader in charge of workforce transformation execution and strategy within Citi's 17k-person Global Functions Technology sector.

Responsibilities include:
* Creation and oversight of the Agile Transformation Office including securing multi-year budget and establishing the office from the ground up, driving best practices in Agile Delivery, and implementing scalable product and budget change across 900 Agile engineering teams
* Successful creation, operationalization, and oversight of the Evergreen Hiring program within Citi Global Functions, designed to consistently and quickly  hire thousands of highly-skilled technical full-time resources over several years in strategic locations
* Member of the Senior  Management Team (SMT) within Citi Global Functions, with direct influence over 17k direct and indirect staff, and direct management responsibility for multiple layers of Banking Directors and Senior Vice Presidents 
*  Developed organizational target state and execution path to transition 17.5k vendor resources into a 10k person organization with 80% full-time staff
*  Onboarded  and own $10MM SaaS platform, Agility Health Radar, as the Agile Maturity tool for Global Functions
* Co-created and began implementing a complete $95MM, 1800 person QA to QE transformation including budget ask, strategic vendor selection, executive change management and execution

Solution Ownership - Charlotte-based client-facing leadership role combines (multiple) technical teams management, Agile implementation, transformation, coaching and best practices, SCRUM Master (coaching), Product and Program Management, Project Management, Change Management, KPI identification and tracking, and Delivery Expert.

Part of the (senior) leadership team for 50MM+, multi-year, AWS-based Oil and Gas pipeline management project. Facilitated SAFe agile project standards/best practices, while managing 4 x 9 -person agile teams with multiple discrete domains. Oversaw resourcing, hiring, product road mapping, delivery (focus on velocity predictability and management) and ongoing discovery across all three teams; acted as SCRUM Master coach, Project and Product Manager Manager, Jira Administrator and problem solving expert.
